data.title: B2 Level Check
data.description: A mixed grammar and usage check to estimate whether the learner is working securely at CEFR B2 level.

sections.explain: Present perfect continuous is 'have been' + -ing for an action continuing up to now: 'have been waiting'. 'have been waited' misuses the participle, and 'am waiting' loses the up-to-now meaning.

words.word: I have been waiting for over an hour.
I have been waited for over an hour.
I am waiting for over an hour.

sections.explain: 'Be about to' + base verb describes the immediate future: 'is about to leave'. It takes 'to' + base verb, not '-ing'.

words.word: The train is about to leave.
The train is about to leaving.
The train is about leaving.

sections.explain: Comparisons of equality use 'as + adjective + as': 'as hard as I expected'. We don't use 'as ... than'.

words.word: The exam was nowhere near as hard than I expected.
The exam was nowhere near so hard than I expected.
The exam was nowhere near as hard as I expected.

sections.explain: 'Should have' + past participle criticises a past action: 'should have told'. 'should have telling' and 'should told' are incorrect.

words.word: You should have told me earlier.
You should told me earlier.
You should have telling me earlier.

sections.explain: The third conditional uses past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have' + participle in the result. Don't use 'would have' in the if-clause or drop 'have' in the result.

words.word: If we would have left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
If we had left earlier, we wouldn't missed the train.

sections.explain: A passive infinitive is 'to be' + past participle: 'expected to be introduced'. 'to introduce' is active, and 'the policy expects' reverses the meaning.

words.word: The new policy expects to be introduced next year.
The new policy is expected to introduce next year.
The new policy is expected to be introduced next year.

sections.explain: Reported commands use 'told + object + (not) to + base verb': 'told us not to enter'. 'don't enter' keeps direct speech, and 'not enter' omits 'to'.

words.word: The officer told us not to enter.
The officer told us don't enter.
The officer told us not enter.

sections.explain: Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas and use 'which', not 'that': 'The report, which was published today, ...'. The commas are required.

words.word: The report, which was published today, is very detailed.
The report which was published today is very detailed.
The report, that was published today, is very detailed.

sections.explain: 'Put off' means to postpone: 'The meeting was put off'. 'put away' means to tidy, and 'put up' has other meanings.

words.word: The meeting was put off until next week.
The meeting was put away until next week.
The meeting was put up until next week.

sections.explain: After a negative adverb like 'never' at the start, subject and auxiliary invert: 'Never have I seen'. The subject can't stay before 'have', and the participle 'seen' is needed, not 'saw'.

words.word: Never have I saw such a beautiful sunset.
Never I have seen such a beautiful sunset.
Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.
